title: dissectors: Add support for S7Comm-Plus protocol
description:
This protocol is for the current family of Siemens programmable logic controllers (PLC), like S7-1200 and S7-1500.
It uses Iso-On-TCP as transport layer, similar to the old S7 protocol. There is no official documentation available.
TLS encryption with newer firmware versions is optional, where the Iso-On-TCP payload is encrypted.

The dissector has a history of development as an external plugin [1] since 2014.
The protocol has changed in some details during the PLC firmware iterations, but for now it seems to be relatively stable.

[1] https://sourceforge.net/projects/s7commwireshark/

How much fuzz testing has been done on this thing? I hope a lot, especially with ZLIB decompression in there. How about zip-bomb prevention?

Just started fuzz testing (never used this before), and have one capture where it failed. Working on this. I've looked at a few other dissectors using Zlib decompression, and haven't seen special handling. Do you know one where I can take a look at?

After the last change, I made about 3000 fuzz tests on 32 captures with complete 12 MB.

It happened 2 times that I get an error like:
Return value: 0
Dissector bug: 0
Date and time: Fri Dec  5 15:45:53 UTC 2025
Build host information:
CYGWIN_NT-10.0-19045 3.6.5-1.x86_64 2025-10-09 17:21 UTC x86_64

Command and args: run/tshark --log-fatal-domains=UTF-8  -nVxr
**
ERROR:C:\Development\wireshark\wsutil\wmem\wmem_allocator_strict.c:65:wmem_strict_block_check_canaries: 'canary[i] == WMEM_CANARY_VALUE' should be TRUE

But the affected and stored fuzzed capture file I can load in wireshark or in thark again without any problems.

I'm running the tests in a Windows 10 VM under cygwin.

The fuzz tester builds with memory checking features enabled, IIRC. In effect it adds 'canaries' around your memory allocations and checks them. Apparently the dissector writes in unallocated memory, causing these errors to be reported. These can be very elusive bugs in normal circumstances (i.e., normal builds), so that's probably why you're not seeing it. But they definitely have to be fixed.

The fuzz test script at least as I use it, uses the tshark.exe from my build directory. Nothing special as far as I can see. And I call tshark with the same options on the affected capture as the script does, and no problem. And with Wireshark GUI I can click on every packet without seeing anything on the Wireshark console.

It doesn't need to be recompiled to change the memory allocation. There's an environment variable that the script uses that changes the memory allocator. Details here: https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/doc/README.wmem

Try launching Wireshark setting WIRESHARK_DEBUG_WMEM_OVERRIDE to strict for example.

There are some additional checks that can be done by compiling with AddressSanitizer, which causes the program to run more slowly.

With WIRESHARK_DEBUG_WMEM_OVERRIDE=strict I was able to test this with tshark from the commandline.

I was able to strip down the fuzzed capture to 8 frames. It has something to do with my reassembly functions. Curiously if I change one constant from 1 to 100, then the problem goes away (at least with 3 problematic captures I've saved).
It's in line 5412, from:
#define CONV_STATE_FIRST       1
to
#define CONV_STATE_FIRST       100
and all is fine. Changing the constant to 4 works as well.
Should we move the discussion to the dev mailing list?

Made some tests with Ubuntu GCC, where the behaviour is the same as with Windows. My state "CONV_STATE_FIRST" is only written, but never compared. And I'm only following the NULL-pointer once. I have no idea why just changing the constant values might fix any problem. I'm renumbering the state values from 0 to 4 instead of -1 to 3, and run some fuzz tests over night in parallel under Ubuntu and Windows.
Can you attach a sample capture file here so that someone else can take a look at fuzzing?

I now renumbered my constants CONV_STATE_NEW=1,NOFRAG=1,FIRST=2,INNER=3,LAST=4, and ran over 60000 fuzz tests with Ubuntu and 11000 with Windows without problems. With the problematic numbering, the error only occurs in my main dissect function dissect_s7commp(). I've commented calling any of my other dissect function, thus the problem must have something to do with the conversation / reassembly memory management.

I've attached a sample S7CommPlus file, and the fuzzed one where I get the wmem error, reduced to the minimal amount of frames. My main dissect function dissect_s7commp() is only called on frame 2. If you remove frames 3-8 from the capture, the problem goes away.

[fuzz-minimal-with-wmem-canary-error.pcapng](/uploads/0d47f51d926933a23afd0ddea40de940/fuzz-minimal-with-wmem-canary-error.pcapng)[S7CommPlus_Sample_WinCC73_1500Plcsim_ASAlarms.pcapng](/uploads/9799f4bf05d301a0187f0d5ee8553754/S7CommPlus_Sample_WinCC73_1500Plcsim_ASAlarms.pcapng)

John, thank you for analyzing this problem. Is it ok to distinguish the standard and ssl conversations, by using the port_b for this, and setting the options parameter to 0? So the port_b gets into the algorithm, and then I'd use port_b=1 for standard, and port_b=2 for ssl conversations.

It's a big dissector so I'd have to look closely, but usually my approach would be either having one larger state structure that contains all the information, both for the protocol with and without TLS, or having two different proto_id numbers (possibly one from `proto_register_protocol_in_name_only`.)

Based on [what gitlab tells me is the current state of the dissector](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/0242cd05a3c45bd1f67f287e9e2f13019eb111f9/epan/dissectors/packet-s7comm_plus.c), you appear to be going the PINO route, which I think makes things clear and easier to track. Has it resulted in resolving the fuzz test issues?
requested changes
The main problem I have for now, is that recursion is not allowed. This would need a complete redesign of the dissector to change this.

It's possible to disable the recursion failures from clang-tidy. Search for `// NOLINTNEXTLINE(misc-no-recursion)` in other files to see how it's done. Just be very careful that overflow isn't occurring.

Can you look this clang analyzer warning ?

`packet-s7comm_plus.c:9036:21: warning: Value stored to 'array_lowerbounds' is never read [deadcode.DeadStores]`

`packet-s7comm_plus.c:9039:21: warning: Value stored to 'array_elementcount' is never read [deadcode.DeadStores]`

`packet-s7comm_plus.c:9044:21: warning: Value stored to 'array_elementcount' is never read [deadcode.DeadStores]`

`packet-s7comm_plus.c:11632:45: warning: Access to field 'start_frame' results in a dereference of a null pointer (loaded from variable 'conversation_state') [core.NullDereference]`

`packet-s7comm_plus.c:11808:45: warning: Access to field 'start_frame' results in a dereference of a null pointer (loaded from variable 'ssl_conversation_state') [core.NullDereference]`

`packet-s7comm_plus.c:11861:25: warning: Access to field 'reasm_state' results in a dereference of a null pointer (loaded from variable 'ssl_conversation_state') [core.NullDereference]`

`packet-s7comm_plus.c:11865:25: warning: Value stored to 'fd_head' is never read [deadcode.DeadStores]`

`packet-s7comm_plus.c:11877:57: warning: Access to field 'reasm_state' results in a dereference of a null pointer (loaded from variable 'ssl_conversation_state') [core.NullDereference]`

How reliable are these NullDereference warnings? In the ssl part it can never happen in my opinion (at least not if wmem_new would fail) as all access is done in a "!pinfo->fd->visited" path.

The first 2 NullDereference warnings are true, but in reality will never happen, if storing the data with p_add_proto_data() in the first pass was successfull. Other dissectors sometimes add a DISSECTOR_ASSERT() check after this. But all smells like it has something to do with the other wmem error.

Is there any overlap with the S7Comm protocol for shared code (and/or value_strings)?
Also, the proto_reg_handoff_s7commp() and proto_register_s7commp() functions should be at the bottom of the file.  It also has the benefit of then needing less forward declarations.

The forward declarations do all the dissectors as far as I can see. There's a comment that it's required to prevent -Wmissing-prototypes warnings.
The S7comm-plus and S7comm protocol have almost nothing in common on protocol layer, only they use both IsoOnTCP as transport layer. The first versions of the S7-1200 controllers used parts of the symbolic addressing (access by a series of IDs and not with a memory address) inside the old S7comm protocol, which is also in the S7comm-plus protocol. But I don't think it's good idea to share this little part, because inside the S7comm-plus protocol the IDs mean much more.

The base (non-fuzzed) sample file [mentioned above](https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/22606#note_2937142833) is giving me a malformed packet on packet number 110. The same section of data appears to be being parsed multiple times in multiple different ways. This could be a recursion issue, or a loop index or offset variable that's too small and is overflowing. I'm still investigating. It's challenging since I don't know much about the protocol so I can't tell what values are potentially bad.
